Understanding Circuit Breakers

By Ada Example, March 3, 2026

A circuit breaker stops a client from hammering a dependency that is already failing. After a run of consecutive failures the breaker opens, and calls fail fast for a cooldown period instead of piling up behind slow timeouts. When the cooldown ends, a single trial call decides whether the breaker closes again.

Why fail fast

Timeouts are expensive. A request that waits thirty seconds for a dead upstream holds a connection, a worker slot and the caller's patience. Failing fast frees those resources and lets a fallback path take over, which is usually what the user wanted in the first place.

Read more in the guide to retries with jitter and the pattern catalog.

Choosing thresholds

Pick the failure threshold from the error rate you can tolerate, not from a round number. Five consecutive failures is a common default because it filters out isolated blips while still reacting within seconds when a dependency goes down hard. Cooldowns between thirty seconds and a few minutes work for most services.

  • Count only failures that a retry would not fix.
  • Never open the breaker for the last remaining option.
  • Emit a metric every time the state changes.
if (breaker.isOpen(provider)) skip(provider);
